BUYER NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK (Wattlebridge Holdings) - our internal positions for Project Kestrel.
Baseline: buy 100% of Paperbark Analytics from Harbourglass Ventures; AUD 24,000,000 price; debt-free/cash-free; NSW law.
- General Warranty cap: starting position 25% / AUD 6,000,000. A 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap is a conditional fallback usable ONLY with prior written authority from buyer principal Amelia Frost, identifying the draft; none has been given.
- Thresholds: de minimis AUD 5,000; aggregate basket AUD 50,000, seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded.
- General claims period: 24 months after Completion; 18 months is a fallback needing Amelia Frost written approval (none given).
- Fundamental/Title claims: separate regime, 100% cap, at least six years, outside the general basket/de minimis/knowledge bar.
- Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct: carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive this.
- Disclosure: require specific fair disclosure; reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.
- Buyer knowledge: delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.
- Bluefen consent: require effective consent AND evidence its conditions are satisfied before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavours alone is insufficient for a material customer consent.
- Riverlark: require current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds and effective security releases; a post-completion release needs an irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval.
- Employee bonuses: DD-005 AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or seller-funded; the funds flow must not silently exclude them.
- Ironquay IP: broaden the narrow indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; the AUD 180,000 is not independently verified either way.
- Export/privacy incident (DD-006): preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume NO confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction.
- Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000): assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.
- Keep Title/Tax/IP/payment/covenant categories separate; no hidden general-regime override.
- Title: require independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 register is a supplied internal source, not independent proof.
- Tax/IP terms remain OPEN; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution.

To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

## Executive view

The Seller’s package materially departs from the Buyer playbook on nearly every important liability and completion-protection point. The statements that provisions are “STANDARD”, “FINAL”, agreed at principal level or previously cleared should be disregarded unless independently confirmed by the Buyer team. They do not constitute Amelia Frost’s required written authority.

In particular:

- **20% general cap and 18-month claim period are not authorised fallbacks**;
- the proposed thresholds are substantially worse than our position;
- title/fundamental claims cannot be folded into the general regime;
- fraud and deliberate wrongdoing must remain outside every contractual limitation;
- Bluefen and Riverlark remain unresolved completion risks;
- the funds flow does not transparently address the employee bonuses;
- the general disclosure and Buyer-knowledge provisions are unacceptable;
- Ironquay requires broader protection; and
- Tax and IP remain open, notwithstanding the Seller’s assertion that they are settled.

We should request the complete SPA and schedules in mark-up. The summary cannot be relied on to identify hidden cross-application of limitations.

---

# Material departures and recommended pushback

## 1. General warranty cap

**Seller position:** 20% of price, or AUD 4.8 million.

**Playbook:** 25%, or AUD 6 million. A 20% cap is available only with prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the relevant draft. No such authority exists.

**Concern:** The Seller is presenting an unauthorised fallback as an agreed position. This is a material reduction in recourse of AUD 1.2 million.

**Pushback:**

- Reinstate the **AUD 6 million / 25% general warranty cap**.
- State expressly that no approval has been given for the 20% fallback.
- Ensure this general cap applies only to properly defined general Warranty Claims, not title, tax, IP indemnity, payment obligations, completion adjustments, covenants or fraud-related claims.

## 2. De minimis and basket

**Seller position:**

- AUD 25,000 de minimis;
- AUD 250,000 deductible basket; and
- only loss above the basket is recoverable.

**Playbook:**

- AUD 5,000 de minimis;
- AUD 50,000 aggregate basket; and
- once exceeded, liability is from the **first dollar**.

**Concern:** The Seller’s formulation increases both thresholds fivefold and converts the basket from a tipping basket to a deductible. It could eliminate recovery for numerous individually meaningful claims and leaves the Buyer bearing the first AUD 250,000 even after systemic breaches are established.

**Pushback:** Restore:

- AUD 5,000 de minimis;
- AUD 50,000 tipping basket;
- recovery of all qualifying losses from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded.

The thresholds must not apply to title/fundamental claims, fraud, specific indemnities, tax claims, completion payments, debt claims or covenant enforcement.

## 3. General warranty claims period

**Seller position:** 18 months after Completion.

**Playbook:** 24 months. Eighteen months requires Amelia Frost’s prior written approval, which has not been given.

**Concern:** Many warranty issues, including customer, accounting, employee, compliance and recurring SaaS matters, may not emerge until after a full reporting or renewal cycle.

**Pushback:** Restore the **24-month** notification period. Review the full clause to ensure a timely notification preserves the claim until final determination and that there is no unduly short period for commencing proceedings.

## 4. Fundamental and title claims

**Seller position:** Apply the same general cap and time limits to capacity and title warranties “for administrative simplicity.”

**Playbook:** Separate regime comprising:

- 100% of purchase price cap;
- at least six years;
- outside the general de minimis, basket and Buyer-knowledge exclusion.

**Concern:** Ownership of the shares, authority to sell and freedom from encumbrances are foundational to the transaction. Administrative convenience is not a justification for transferring defective-title risk to the Buyer.

**Pushback:** Create an express separate regime for title, ownership, capacity and authority claims:

- cap of **100% of the purchase price**;
- claim period of at least **six years**;
- no de minimis or basket;
- no Buyer-knowledge defence;
- no dilution through general disclosure; and
- no exclusive-remedy restriction that prevents proprietary, equitable or specific-performance relief.

## 5. Fraud and deliberate wrongdoing

**Seller position:** Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all claims “of any nature.” No express fraud carve-out is identified.

**Playbook:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct must be carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions to the maximum extent enforceable. This position cannot be waived.

**Concern:** “All Claims of any nature” could purport to protect the Seller even where it intentionally misleads the Buyer or conceals a problem. It may also allow limitations to apply indirectly through definitions or cross-references.

**Pushback:** Add an overriding provision stating that no limitation or exclusion applies to fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation, wilful concealment or deliberate misconduct. It should prevail over:

- caps and thresholds;
- time limits;
- exclusive-remedy language;
- non-reliance and entire-agreement provisions;
- disclosure and knowledge defences; and
- any limitation incorporated into an indemnity or covenant.

Also ensure the drafting does not limit the carve-out only to fraud personally committed by the corporate Seller if that would exclude relevant conduct of its officers or agents.

## 6. Overbroad application of the general limitations regime

**Seller position:** Any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly excluded; exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all claims.

**Concern:** This reverses the appropriate allocation. It risks silently subjecting title, tax, IP, specific indemnities, completion payments and covenant claims to the general warranty cap, thresholds and time bar. It could also interfere with claims for debt, specific performance, injunctions or completion adjustments.

**Pushback:**

- Limit the general regime expressly to **general Warranty Claims**.
- Draft separate, affirmative rules for title, tax, IP and each specific indemnity.
- Exclude payment obligations, price adjustments, debt claims, covenants and completion obligations.
- Preserve specific performance, injunctions and other appropriate equitable remedies.
- Require clear category-by-category caps and periods rather than a broad “all Claims” rule.

## 7. Disclosure standard

**Seller position:** General disclosure of every matter contained or referred to in the data room, the Accounts, statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records.

**Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure; no whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.

**Concern:** The Buyer should not be treated as knowing every inference that might be derived from a large document set. “Contained or referred to” may incorporate additional material not actually supplied and shift the burden of identifying breaches to the Buyer.

**Pushback:**

- Delete paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 as general disclosures.
- Require each exception to be **specifically and fairly disclosed**, in sufficient detail to identify the nature and reasonably apparent scope of the matter.
- Tie each specific disclosure to the particular warranty or warranties qualified.
- Prevent disclosure from qualifying title, capacity, fraud, covenants, completion conditions or specific indemnities.
- State that mere document availability, a public filing or a reference to another document does not constitute fair disclosure.

The specific factual disclosures may remain for assessment, but they should not validate the general disclosure framework.

## 8. Buyer knowledge exclusion

**Seller position:** No claim for anything known by the Buyer or its advisers, including matters discoverable from the data room or public records.

**Playbook:** Delete blanket Buyer-knowledge exclusions. Any knowledge formulation must not excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities. Warranty knowledge qualifiers should use named Seller knowledge persons and reasonable enquiry.

**Concern:** The provision includes constructive and imputed knowledge across an undefined group of advisers. It would undermine the disclosure bargain and potentially reward incomplete or obscure disclosure.

**Pushback:**

- Delete clause 8.3.
- Reject “discoverable,” deemed, constructive and adviser-imputed knowledge.
- If any narrow actual-knowledge compromise is later considered, it should identify specific Buyer individuals, exclude adviser knowledge and apply only to actual conscious knowledge—not what the Buyer ought to have found.
- In all cases exclude title, capacity, authority, fraud, deliberate concealment and specific indemnities.
- Where Seller warranties need knowledge qualifiers, use named Seller knowledge persons subject to reasonable enquiry.

## 9. Bluefen customer consent

**Facts disclosed:** Bluefen represents approximately AUD 3.6 million FY26 revenue, around 30%. No final written consent or evidence that clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied has been supplied.

**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours, with the condition treated as satisfied on delivery of written consent.

**Playbook:** Effective consent and evidence that all associated conditions are satisfied before Completion. Reasonable endeavours and consent-on-delivery are insufficient.

**Concern:** A document labelled “consent” may be conditional, revocable, incomplete or impose adverse commercial terms. Given Bluefen’s revenue concentration, this is a material completion risk.

**Pushback:**

- Make receipt of an **effective and unconditional consent**, in form and substance satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably, a condition precedent.
- Require evidence before Completion that all clause 11.3 conditions have been satisfied.
- Require disclosure of all communications and proposed conditions.
- Prevent satisfaction where the consent changes pricing, term, service obligations, termination rights or other material terms without Buyer approval.
- No deemed satisfaction merely upon delivery and no reasonable-endeavours-only standard.

## 10. Riverlark debt and security releases

**Facts disclosed:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding; no repayment or final security discharge has been supplied.

**Seller position:** Release to be provided after Completion.

**Playbook:** Current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds and effective releases. A post-Completion release requires both an irrevocable undertaking and Amelia Frost’s approval; no approval exists.

**Concern:** The Buyer must not acquire the Company while Riverlark debt or security remains outstanding or while release depends only on the Seller’s post-Completion performance.

**Pushback:**

- Obtain a current lender payout letter covering principal, interest, fees and per-diem amounts.
- Pay Riverlark directly from Completion funds.
- Require simultaneous, effective discharge and release of all Company and share security, guarantees and claims.
- Obtain applicable registration discharge documents and evidence of lodgement/registration.
- Do not accept a post-Completion release. If one becomes unavoidable, it requires an irrevocable lender undertaking in agreed form and Amelia Frost’s written approval.

## 11. Completion bonuses and on-costs

**Facts disclosed:** AUD 420,000 of conditional Completion bonuses are absent from the draft funds flow. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs are not quantified.

**Seller position:** They are “a matter for the Seller” and need not be separately itemised.

**Playbook:** The AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or otherwise Seller-funded.

**Concern:** The current drafting could leave the Company—and economically the Buyer—funding liabilities triggered by the Seller’s transaction. Saying they are a Seller matter is insufficient if the legal payment obligation remains with the Company.

**Pushback:**

- Quantify all bonuses and applicable superannuation, payroll tax, workers’ compensation impacts and other on-costs.
- Include them expressly in the funds flow and have them funded by the Seller or deducted from Seller proceeds.
- Clarify who is the legal payer and when payment is due.
- Obtain an indemnity for any unprovided bonus or on-cost liability.
- Ensure the amounts are not also captured inconsistently elsewhere in debt, working capital or leakage calculations.

## 12. Ironquay IP

**Facts disclosed:** Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, but this is not independent verification. No receipt or confirmatory assignment is available.

**Seller position:** Indemnity limited to the specific SOW3 payment.

**Playbook:** Broaden the narrow indemnity while preserving the SOW3 cure. The AUD 180,000 is not independently verified in either direction.

**Concern:** Paying AUD 180,000 may not cure all defects. The Buyer needs both ownership/usage rights and protection against losses arising from incomplete transfer, non-payment, infringement or competing rights.

**Pushback:**

- Independently confirm the amount required for cleared payment.
- Provide for direct payment at Completion if that is the agreed cure.
- Require a confirmatory assignment, waiver/consent and evidence that the Company obtains all intended rights free of encumbrances.
- Broaden the indemnity beyond the payment itself to cover losses arising from:
  - failure of transfer or defective title;
  - unpaid fees and related claims;
  - infringement or third-party ownership claims;
  - inability to use, modify, commercialise or license the materials; and
  - costs of remediation or replacement.
- Keep the indemnity outside the general warranty basket and cap, subject to a separately negotiated IP regime.

Do not treat AUD 180,000 as finally established until independently verified.

## 13. Export/privacy incident

**Facts disclosed:** A download link was sent to an unintended external email address and may concern about 1,240 records. Access, exact scope and notification requirements remain unconfirmed.

**Seller position:** Preliminary and not expected to be material.

**Playbook:** Preserve evidence, investigate and provide updates; assume neither a confirmed breach nor a quantified claim or notification obligation.

**Concern:** The Seller’s materiality assessment is unsupported. Equally, the current record does not justify stating that a notifiable breach, harm or fixed loss has occurred.

**Pushback:**

- Require preservation of logs, access records, emails, system metadata and investigation materials.
- Require a properly scoped investigation and regular written updates through Completion.
- Require prompt notification of access evidence, expanded scope, regulator/customer contact or any legal notification analysis.
- Restrict deletion or alteration of relevant records.
- Include an appropriate warranty/covenant concerning accuracy of updates and compliance with agreed incident-response steps.
- Consider a specific indemnity once facts and allocation are clearer, without asserting a confirmed breach or numeric demand now.
- Prevent the Seller’s “not expected to be material” statement from qualifying warranties by itself.

## 14. Sandbar supplier renewals

**Facts disclosed:** Three renewals of AUD 110,000 each, AUD 330,000 aggregate. It is unclear whether they are avoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Playbook:** Assess; no automatic classification as Debt or automatic price deduction.

**Concern:** The Seller’s characterisation is not established by the documents. But the Buyer should not automatically treat the total as debt without understanding timing, accrual and services.

**Pushback:** Obtain:

- contracts and renewal notices;
- service periods and invoice/payment dates;
- termination and cancellation rights;
- evidence of past practice and ordinary-course treatment;
- accounting treatment and whether any amount is accrued, prepaid or overdue; and
- confirmation of whether commitments were entered into consistently with interim operating covenants.

Then determine treatment under the agreed price mechanics. Reserve the Buyer’s position; do not automatically deduct AUD 330,000 or accept it as ordinary course.

## 15. Tax and IP positions

**Seller position:** Both are settled under the general warranty regime.

**Playbook:** Tax and IP remain open. No assumption of unlimited liability or any agreed resolution.

**Concern:** Folding them into the 20%/18-month general regime is neither agreed nor appropriate. Tax claims may emerge after statutory reviews, and IP is central to a SaaS business.

**Pushback:**

- Mark Tax and IP expressly **open**.
- Negotiate separate scopes, caps, limitation periods, conduct-of-claims provisions and exclusions.
- Do not state or imply that liability is unlimited; equally, do not accept the proposed general limitations by default.
- Preserve the Ironquay-specific protection independently from general IP warranties.

## 16. Title evidence

**Seller position:** DD-012 internal share register proves ownership of 100% of the shares.

**Playbook:** Independent evidence of title, ownership, encumbrances and authority. DD-012 is only a supplied internal source.

**Concern:** A company share register is relevant but not independently conclusive as to beneficial disputes, competing rights, options, prior transfers, security interests or authority to sell.

**Pushback:** Require, as applicable:

- current and historical ASIC extracts and lodged share information;
- share certificates and transfer history;
- constitution and relevant shareholder agreements;
- board/shareholder approvals and execution authority;
- PPSR and other relevant security searches;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles, pre-emption rights, trusts or competing interests;
- evidence of release of any share security; and
- completion deliverables updating the register and recording the Buyer as owner.

The title warranties must remain independent of the Buyer’s diligence and the DD-012 disclosure.

## 17. Office lease and Mossvale

The Disclosure Letter appropriately stops short of asserting that either matter requires consent to the share sale:

- DD-007 apparently identifies a lease notification obligation, not necessarily consent.
- DD-009 concerns assignment, which may not be triggered by a share sale.

These points should nevertheless be checked against the full agreements, including any change-of-control, indirect assignment or deemed assignment language. We should not demand consents without a contractual basis, but any required notification should be completed on time and evidenced.

---

# Disclosure Letter drafting points

In addition to deleting general disclosures:

1. Require the disclosure cut-off and index to be fixed, with a complete copy of the disclosed data room preserved.
2. Do not permit later-added documents to be deemed disclosed without Buyer review.
3. Require updates before Completion and Buyer consent to any new material disclosure.
4. Clarify that disclosure only qualifies identified warranties and does not:
   - satisfy a condition precedent;
   - remedy a breach of covenant;
   - reduce a completion payment;
   - qualify an indemnity; or
   - establish Buyer knowledge.
5. Paragraph 1.4 can state that disclosure is not an admission, but it must not prevent the SPA from determining whether the facts constitute a breach or trigger a remedy.

---

# Recommended negotiation priorities

## Completion-critical

1. **Bluefen:** effective consent and satisfaction of all conditions before Completion.
2. **Riverlark:** current payout, direct repayment and simultaneous effective security releases.
3. **Employee bonuses:** fully quantified, expressly funded by the Seller and shown in the funds flow.
4. **Ironquay:** verified cure, effective assignment and broader specific protection.
5. **Title:** independent evidence and effective transfer free of encumbrances.

## Liability package

6. Restore the **25% / AUD 6 million** general cap.
7. Restore the **AUD 5,000 de minimis and AUD 50,000 tipping basket**.
8. Restore the **24-month** general claims period.
9. Put fundamental/title claims under a separate **100% / six-year minimum** regime.
10. Insert the non-waivable fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carve-out.
11. Prevent the general limitations regime from overriding Tax, IP, indemnities, payments and covenants.

## Disclosure and diligence

12. Delete whole-data-room, public-record and constructive disclosure.
13. Delete the blanket Buyer-knowledge exclusion.
14. Continue and document the DD-006 investigation without assuming a confirmed breach or loss.
15. Investigate Sandbar before deciding price-mechanics treatment.
16. Keep Tax and IP expressly open.

No concessions to the 20% cap or 18-month period should be made unless Amelia Frost gives the required written approval identifying the relevant draft.

**Pushback:** Restore the **24-month** notification period. Review the full clause to ensure a timely notification preserves the claim until final determination and that there is no unduly short period for commencing proceedings.

## 4. Fundamental and title claims

**Seller position:** Apply the same general cap and time limits to capacity and title warranties “for administrative simplicity.”

**Playbook:** Separate regime comprising:

- 100% of purchase price cap;
- at least six years;
- outside the general de minimis, basket and Buyer-knowledge exclusion.

**Concern:** Ownership of the shares, authority to sell and freedom from encumbrances are foundational to the transaction. Administrative convenience is not a justification for transferring defective-title risk to the Buyer.

**Pushback:** Create an express separate regime for title, ownership, capacity and authority claims:

- cap of **100% of the purchase price**;
- claim period of at least **six years**;
- no de minimis or basket;
- no Buyer-knowledge defence;
- no dilution through general disclosure; and
- no exclusive-remedy restriction that prevents proprietary, equitable or specific-performance relief.

## 5. Fraud and deliberate wrongdoing

**Seller position:** Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all claims “of any nature.” No express fraud carve-out is identified.

**Playbook:** Fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct must be carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions to the maximum extent enforceable. This position cannot be waived.

**Concern:** “All Claims of any nature” could purport to protect the Seller even where it intentionally misleads the Buyer or conceals a problem. It may also allow limitations to apply indirectly through definitions or cross-references.

**Pushback:** Add an overriding provision stating that no limitation or exclusion applies to fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation, wilful concealment or deliberate misconduct. It should prevail over:

- caps and thresholds;
- time limits;
- exclusive-remedy language;
- non-reliance and entire-agreement provisions;
- disclosure and knowledge defences; and
- any limitation incorporated into an indemnity or covenant.

Also ensure the drafting does not limit the carve-out only to fraud personally committed by the corporate Seller if that would exclude relevant conduct of its officers or agents.

## 6. Overbroad application of the general limitations regime

**Seller position:** Any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly excluded; exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all claims.

**Concern:** This reverses the appropriate allocation. It risks silently subjecting title, tax, IP, specific indemnities, completion payments and covenant claims to the general warranty cap, thresholds and time bar. It could also interfere with claims for debt, specific performance, injunctions or completion adjustments.

**Pushback:**

- Limit the general regime expressly to **general Warranty Claims**.
- Draft separate, affirmative rules for title, tax, IP and each specific indemnity.
- Exclude payment obligations, price adjustments, debt claims, covenants and completion obligations.
- Preserve specific performance, injunctions and other appropriate equitable remedies.
- Require clear category-by-category caps and periods rather than a broad “all Claims” rule.

## 7. Disclosure standard

**Seller position:** General disclosure of every matter contained or referred to in the data room, the Accounts, statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records.

**Playbook:** Specific fair disclosure; no whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.

**Concern:** The Buyer should not be treated as knowing every inference that might be derived from a large document set. “Contained or referred to” may incorporate additional material not actually supplied and shift the burden of identifying breaches to the Buyer.

**Pushback:**

- Delete paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2 as general disclosures.
- Require each exception to be **specifically and fairly disclosed**, in sufficient detail to identify the nature and reasonably apparent scope of the matter.
- Tie each specific disclosure to the particular warranty or warranties qualified.
- Prevent disclosure from qualifying title, capacity, fraud, covenants, completion conditions or specific indemnities.
- State that mere document availability, a public filing or a reference to another document does not constitute fair disclosure.

The specific factual disclosures may remain for assessment, but they should not validate the general disclosure framework.

## 8. Buyer knowledge exclusion

**Seller position:** No claim for anything known by the Buyer or its advisers, including matters discoverable from the data room or public records.

**Playbook:** Delete blanket Buyer-knowledge exclusions. Any knowledge formulation must not excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities. Warranty knowledge qualifiers should use named Seller knowledge persons and reasonable enquiry.

**Concern:** The provision includes constructive and imputed knowledge across an undefined group of advisers. It would undermine the disclosure bargain and potentially reward incomplete or obscure disclosure.

**Pushback:**

- Delete clause 8.3.
- Reject “discoverable,” deemed, constructive and adviser-imputed knowledge.
- If any narrow actual-knowledge compromise is later considered, it should identify specific Buyer individuals, exclude adviser knowledge and apply only to actual conscious knowledge—not what the Buyer ought to have found.
- In all cases exclude title, capacity, authority, fraud, deliberate concealment and specific indemnities.
- Where Seller warranties need knowledge qualifiers, use named Seller knowledge persons subject to reasonable enquiry.

## 9. Bluefen customer consent

**Facts disclosed:** Bluefen represents approximately AUD 3.6 million FY26 revenue, around 30%. No final written consent or evidence that clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied has been supplied.

**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours, with the condition treated as satisfied on delivery of written consent.

**Playbook:** Effective consent and evidence that all associated conditions are satisfied before Completion. Reasonable endeavours and consent-on-delivery are insufficient.

**Concern:** A document labelled “consent” may be conditional, revocable, incomplete or impose adverse commercial terms. Given Bluefen’s revenue concentration, this is a material completion risk.

**Pushback:**

- Make receipt of an **effective and unconditional consent**, in form and substance satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably, a condition precedent.
- Require evidence before Completion that all clause 11.3 conditions have been satisfied.
- Require disclosure of all communications and proposed conditions.
- Prevent satisfaction where the consent changes pricing, term, service obligations, termination rights or other material terms without Buyer approval.
- No deemed satisfaction merely upon delivery and no reasonable-endeavours-only standard.

## 10. Riverlark debt and security releases

**Facts disclosed:** Approximately AUD 3.2 million remains outstanding; no repayment or final security discharge has been supplied.

**Seller position:** Release to be provided after Completion.

**Playbook:** Current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds and effective releases. A post-Completion release requires both an irrevocable undertaking and Amelia Frost’s approval; no approval exists.

**Concern:** The Buyer must not acquire the Company while Riverlark debt or security remains outstanding or while release depends only on the Seller’s post-Completion performance.

**Pushback:**

- Obtain a current lender payout letter covering principal, interest, fees and per-diem amounts.
- Pay Riverlark directly from Completion funds.
- Require simultaneous, effective discharge and release of all Company and share security, guarantees and claims.
- Obtain applicable registration discharge documents and evidence of lodgement/registration.
- Do not accept a post-Completion release. If one becomes unavoidable, it requires an irrevocable lender undertaking in agreed form and Amelia Frost’s written approval.

## 11. Completion bonuses and on-costs

**Facts disclosed:** AUD 420,000 of conditional Completion bonuses are absent from the draft funds flow. Payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs are not quantified.

**Seller position:** They are “a matter for the Seller” and need not be separately itemised.

**Playbook:** The AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or otherwise Seller-funded.

**Concern:** The current drafting could leave the Company—and economically the Buyer—funding liabilities triggered by the Seller’s transaction. Saying they are a Seller matter is insufficient if the legal payment obligation remains with the Company.

**Pushback:**

- Quantify all bonuses and applicable superannuation, payroll tax, workers’ compensation impacts and other on-costs.
- Include them expressly in the funds flow and have them funded by the Seller or deducted from Seller proceeds.
- Clarify who is the legal payer and when payment is due.
- Obtain an indemnity for any unprovided bonus or on-cost liability.
- Ensure the amounts are not also captured inconsistently elsewhere in debt, working capital or leakage calculations.

## 12. Ironquay IP

**Facts disclosed:** Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, but this is not independent verification. No receipt or confirmatory assignment is available.

**Seller position:** Indemnity limited to the specific SOW3 payment.

**Playbook:** Broaden the narrow indemnity while preserving the SOW3 cure. The AUD 180,000 is not independently verified in either direction.

**Concern:** Paying AUD 180,000 may not cure all defects. The Buyer needs both ownership/usage rights and protection against losses arising from incomplete transfer, non-payment, infringement or competing rights.

**Pushback:**

- Independently confirm the amount required for cleared payment.
- Provide for direct payment at Completion if that is the agreed cure.
- Require a confirmatory assignment, waiver/consent and evidence that the Company obtains all intended rights free of encumbrances.
- Broaden the indemnity beyond the payment itself to cover losses arising from:
  - failure of transfer or defective title;
  - unpaid fees and related claims;
  - infringement or third-party ownership claims;
  - inability to use, modify, commercialise or license the materials; and
  - costs of remediation or replacement.
- Keep the indemnity outside the general warranty basket and cap, subject to a separately negotiated IP regime.

Do not treat AUD 180,000 as finally established until independently verified.

## 13. Export/privacy incident

**Facts disclosed:** A download link was sent to an unintended external email address and may concern about 1,240 records. Access, exact scope and notification requirements remain unconfirmed.

**Seller position:** Preliminary and not expected to be material.

**Playbook:** Preserve evidence, investigate and provide updates; assume neither a confirmed breach nor a quantified claim or notification obligation.

**Concern:** The Seller’s materiality assessment is unsupported. Equally, the current record does not justify stating that a notifiable breach, harm or fixed loss has occurred.

**Pushback:**

- Require preservation of logs, access records, emails, system metadata and investigation materials.
- Require a properly scoped investigation and regular written updates through Completion.
- Require prompt notification of access evidence, expanded scope, regulator/customer contact or any legal notification analysis.
- Restrict deletion or alteration of relevant records.
- Include an appropriate warranty/covenant concerning accuracy of updates and compliance with agreed incident-response steps.
- Consider a specific indemnity once facts and allocation are clearer, without asserting a confirmed breach or numeric demand now.
- Prevent the Seller’s “not expected to be material” statement from qualifying warranties by itself.

## 14. Sandbar supplier renewals

**Facts disclosed:** Three renewals of AUD 110,000 each, AUD 330,000 aggregate. It is unclear whether they are avoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Playbook:** Assess; no automatic classification as Debt or automatic price deduction.

**Concern:** The Seller’s characterisation is not established by the documents. But the Buyer should not automatically treat the total as debt without understanding timing, accrual and services.

**Pushback:** Obtain:

- contracts and renewal notices;
- service periods and invoice/payment dates;
- termination and cancellation rights;
- evidence of past practice and ordinary-course treatment;
- accounting treatment and whether any amount is accrued, prepaid or overdue; and
- confirmation of whether commitments were entered into consistently with interim operating covenants.

Then determine treatment under the agreed price mechanics. Reserve the Buyer’s position; do not automatically deduct AUD 330,000 or accept it as ordinary course.

## 15. Tax and IP positions

**Seller position:** Both are settled under the general warranty regime.

**Playbook:** Tax and IP remain open. No assumption of unlimited liability or any agreed resolution.

**Concern:** Folding them into the 20%/18-month general regime is neither agreed nor appropriate. Tax claims may emerge after statutory reviews, and IP is central to a SaaS business.

**Pushback:**

- Mark Tax and IP expressly **open**.
- Negotiate separate scopes, caps, limitation periods, conduct-of-claims provisions and exclusions.
- Do not state or imply that liability is unlimited; equally, do not accept the proposed general limitations by default.
- Preserve the Ironquay-specific protection independently from general IP warranties.

## 16. Title evidence

**Seller position:** DD-012 internal share register proves ownership of 100% of the shares.

**Playbook:** Independent evidence of title, ownership, encumbrances and authority. DD-012 is only a supplied internal source.

**Concern:** A company share register is relevant but not independently conclusive as to beneficial disputes, competing rights, options, prior transfers, security interests or authority to sell.

**Pushback:** Require, as applicable:

- current and historical ASIC extracts and lodged share information;
- share certificates and transfer history;
- constitution and relevant shareholder agreements;
- board/shareholder approvals and execution authority;
- PPSR and other relevant security searches;
- confirmation of no options, convertibles, pre-emption rights, trusts or competing interests;
- evidence of release of any share security; and
- completion deliverables updating the register and recording the Buyer as owner.

The title warranties must remain independent of the Buyer’s diligence and the DD-012 disclosure.

## 17. Office lease and Mossvale

The Disclosure Letter appropriately stops short of asserting that either matter requires consent to the share sale:

- DD-007 apparently identifies a lease notification obligation, not necessarily consent.
- DD-009 concerns assignment, which may not be triggered by a share sale.

These points should nevertheless be checked against the full agreements, including any change-of-control, indirect assignment or deemed assignment language. We should not demand consents without a contractual basis, but any required notification should be completed on time and evidenced.

# Disclosure Letter drafting points

In addition to deleting general disclosures:

1. Require the disclosure cut-off and index to be fixed, with a complete copy of the disclosed data room preserved.
2. Do not permit later-added documents to be deemed disclosed without Buyer review.
3. Require updates before Completion and Buyer consent to any new material disclosure.
4. Clarify that disclosure only qualifies identified warranties and does not:
   - satisfy a condition precedent;
   - remedy a breach of covenant;
   - reduce a completion payment;
   - qualify an indemnity; or
   - establish Buyer knowledge.
5. Paragraph 1.4 can state that disclosure is not an admission, but it must not prevent the SPA from determining whether the facts constitute a breach or trigger a remedy.
